tip: 'Aus' always takes the dative, so the adjective ends in '-en': 'aus einer großen Tasse'.
'Gut' has the irregular comparative 'besser', never 'guter'; for than, use 'als': 'besser als'.
For body parts German uses a dative reflexive plus the article, not a possessive: 'wasche mir die Hände'.
'Sich merken', with the dative 'mir', means to commit something to memory: 'mir das Passwort einfach nicht merken'.
'Sich schneiden' uses 'in' plus the accusative for the body part affected: 'in den Finger geschnitten'.
'Ans' is 'an' + 'das', and direction toward takes the accusative: 'ans Meer'.
'Ins' is the contraction of 'in' + 'das', and motion into takes the accusative: 'ins Fenster'.
'Hinter' takes the accusative for movement to a spot: 'hinter die Tür'.
'Stellen' sets something upright, a movement, so 'auf' takes the accusative: 'auf den Tisch'.
'Legen' is a movement verb, so 'in' takes the accusative: 'legt das Baby in sein Bettchen'.
'Sich erinnern' normally pairs with 'an' plus the accusative: 'erinnert sich an ihren ersten Schultag'.
'Sich ärgern' takes 'über' plus the accusative for what annoys you: 'ärgert sich über die ständigen Verspätungen'.
Countries used without an article take 'nach' for 'to': 'nach Spanien'.
A stretch of time goes in the accusative with no preposition: 'den ganzen Abend' = the whole evening long.
'Sich freuen auf' is looking forward to something ahead: 'freue mich auf das Wiedersehen'; 'über' is for something already here.
'Am wenigsten' is the superlative used after a verb, built with 'am' plus the '-sten' ending: it means 'the least'.
'Sich kümmern' takes 'um' plus the accusative for who you look after: 'um ihren alten Kater'.
Here 'ruhig' is a softening particle meaning 'go ahead, feel free': 'kannst dir ruhig ein Stück Kuchen nehmen'.
'Sich nähern' takes a dative object directly, with no preposition: 'dem Ende'.
'Vor' takes the dative for location: 'vor der Tür'.
'Ob' (whether) sends the verb to the end: 'ob das Geschäft sonntags geöffnet ist' closes with 'ist'.
'Da' means since/because, like 'weil', and sends the verb to the end: 'da das Wetter zu schlecht war'.
For means of transport, use 'mit' plus the dative: 'mit dem Taxi' means by taxi.
'Zum' is 'zu' plus 'dem'. Use 'zu' plus the dative to show going to a place: 'zum Supermarkt'.
German usually treats the hair on your head as plural, so it is 'Haare', and the adjectives take '-e': 'lange blonde Haare'.
'Nachbar' adds '-n' in every case except the nominative singular, giving 'einen netten Nachbarn'.
'Hoch' drops its 'c' when an ending is added, so it becomes 'hohen' in 'die hohen Berge'.
After 'ein' with a neuter noun, the adjective ends in '-es': 'ein weißes Pferd'.
German adjectives double as adverbs with no extra ending: 'schnell' means both quick and quickly.
'Für' always takes the accusative: 'für ihre Rechte'.
